# Surveying, levelling and triangulation (`surveying_triangulation`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/math.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Mathematics & measurement (`math`)
- Deps: helped by geometry_proof, trigonometry, telescope, logarithms, magnetic_compass
- Core idea: Land is measured with a chain or rods for distance, a sighting device for straight lines and angles, and a level (a water trough or plumb line) for height. Triangulation avoids measuring long distances on the ground: measure one baseline very carefully, sight a distant point from both ends, and the two angles fix the triangle; each new side serves as the baseline of the next triangle. The work can be done by calculation with sine tables or drawn directly to scale on a plane table. Errors are caught by measuring all three angles and closing the chain of triangles on a second measured line.
- Pitfalls:
  - Measuring along the slope and using it as horizontal distance.
  - Choosing long thin triangles, in which a small error of angle becomes a large error of position.
  - Trusting a single measurement of the baseline; every later distance inherits its error.
  - Relying on the compass needle for angles without allowing for declination and nearby iron.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2100 BC – field plans with measured sides and computed areas on Ur III tablets; egypt: from the 3rd millennium BC – rope-stretchers remeasure fields after the Nile flood; pyramids are levelled and oriented to a fraction of a degree; greece: c. 530 BC – Eupalinos' tunnel on Samos is dug from both ends and meets; 1st c. AD Hero of Alexandria, Dioptra, a sighting instrument for angles and levelling; rome: from the 4th–3rd c. BC – surveyors (agrimensores) lay out roads, aqueducts and land grids with groma and chorobates; china: AD 263 – Liu Hui, Haidao suanjing, heights and distances by double sightings; 3rd c. Pei Xiu's rules for scale maps; islamic: c. 1020 – al-Biruni derives the Earth's radius from the dip of the horizon seen from a mountain at Nandana; europe: 1533 – Gemma Frisius describes triangulation; 1551–1571 plane table and theodolite (Foullon, Digges); 1615–1617 Snellius triangulates a meridian arc; 1620 Gunter's chain; 1669–1670 Picard with telescopic sights; 1744–1793 the Cassini survey of France
- Read:
  - Gemma Frisius, Libellus de locorum describendorum ratione (1533)
  - M. J. T. Lewis, Surveying Instruments of Greece and Rome (2001)
